rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its strongest line, "Hugging Face gives the model away and charges $50 a seat for the hub around it," is clean, sourced, and immediately pitchable. B has real strategic instincts, but "Two million models, and no easy way to know which ones are safe to use" turns a governance hunch into a headline before the update gives it evidence. That is how a smart angle gets itself fired in edit.
gaps_in_A: "Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the first angle; this is business-model/pricing, not funding.

"A 1.8B model that runs on a phone with the network off, under a license that lets you ship it" is viable, but still thin until there is named-device performance and at least one real builder using it.
The business-model angle should ask whether Apache 2.0 applies only to weights or also to training code and supporting artifacts; that licensing detail matters.
"Decay: 24hr" on the benchmark angle is too harsh if the model and eval harness are public; reproducibility stories can breathe for days.
gaps_in_B: "A Fortune 100 manufacturer is running Hugging Face models behind its own firewall" overstates the update. The facts say early enterprise customer and private hosting, not behind its own firewall.
"Two million models, and no easy way to know which ones are safe to use" invents the safety gap. The update gives scale, not unsafe models or missing provenance.
"which is a commercial admission that pulling arbitrary weights is a governance problem" is inference stacked on inference from SSO, audit logs, and private hosting.
B keeps an angle it admits is weak: "This is the thinnest angle in the set." Then cut it. The editor will.
